content.title: About
content.content: Beans and white rice are a classic combination of legumes and grains used in cuisines worldwide. Beans provide protein, fiber, and micronutrients, while white rice supplies quick‑digesting carbohydrates for energy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The bean‑rice pairing is considered a complete protein source because together they supply all essential amino acids.
Dried beans can be stored for several years, and rice can last up to a year when kept dry.
In many cultures beans and rice are cooked together in one pot, enhancing flavor and simplifying preparation.
White rice is often fortified with vitamins and iron to replace nutrients lost during milling.

items.title: Rich plant protein
items.content: Beans contain about 20 g of protein per 100 g, making them a key protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber in beans promotes regular bowel movements and helps stabilize blood sugar levels.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: White rice is rapidly digested, providing a fast glucose boost, especially useful after intense exercise.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: Beans are a good source of iron and magnesium, essential for blood formation and muscle function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Both beans and white rice are naturally low in saturated fat, fitting well into low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Beans contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption; soaking and sprouting help mitigate this.

items.title: Lectins
items.content: Certain beans have lectins that may cause gastrointestinal discomfort if not cooked thoroughly.

items.title: High glycemic index of rice
items.content: White rice has a high glycemic index, which can cause rapid blood sugar spikes in people with diabetes.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small percentage of individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soak beans for 6–8 hours, then boil until tender. Rinse white rice and cook with a 1:2 rice‑to‑water ratio. Combine them in salads, soups, pilafs, or as a side dish to meat and vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 2 years. Keep white rice in a sealed package away from moisture and light for up to 12 months. Discard any beans or rice that develop off‑odors, mold, or insect infestation.

content.title: About
content.content: Gruyère is a Swiss semi-hard cheese with a nutty, slightly sweet flavor and characteristic "eyes". Made from cow’s milk in the Fribourg‑Vaud region, it is aged from 6 to 24 months. The cheese has a dense, slightly grainy texture and an aroma that deepens with age.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Gruyère takes its name from the Swiss town of Gruyères, where production began in the 12th century.
Traditional aging involves regular turning and cleaning of the rind.
The cheese is a staple in fondue, raclette, and classic French dishes such as quiche.
There are more than 30 official varieties of Gruyère, each with a different aging period.
Gruyère holds a Protected Designation of Origin (AOP) status, guaranteeing its authenticity.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Calcium in Gruyère supports strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: The cheese provides high‑quality dairy protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Gruyère contains vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for the nervous system and energy metabolism.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: In moderate amounts, the cheese contributes beneficial fatty acids to a balanced diet.

items.title: Probiotic bacteria
items.content: Fermentation introduces beneficial microbes that can support gut health.

items.title: Lactose
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after consuming Gruyère.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The cheese is relatively salty, so individuals with hypertension should limit portions.

items.title: Milk‑protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have an allergic reaction to casein.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Gruyère is calorie‑dense, so it should be eaten in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Gruyère is perfect grated over pasta, salads, casseroles, and sandwiches. It can be served in thin slices with fruit, nuts, or as part of a cheese board. For fondue, cut the cheese into cubes and melt slowly with white wine.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store Gruyère in its original packaging or wrapped in parchment paper inside an airtight container in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C. For longer storage, wrap it in aluminum foil and keep it in a cool cellar. Before use, remove any dry rind.

content.title: About
content.content: Green beans cooked Szechuan-style are tender bean pods quickly stir‑fried with aromatic spices such as Szechuan peppercorns, garlic, ginger and soy sauce. The dish delivers a characteristic spicy‑numbing flavor and a crisp texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Szechuan peppercorns contain hydroxy‑α‑sanshool, which creates a tingling, numbing sensation in the mouth.
Traditionally the beans are cooked only a few minutes to keep them crunchy.
In China the dish is often served as a side to rice or noodles.
Szechuan cuisine is famous for its bold combination of heat and fragrant spices.
Green beans are a good source of plant protein and dietary fiber.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A serving provides about 35 kcal, making it suitable for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B6 and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides iron, magnesium and potassium, which support heart and muscle function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Szechuan pepper and ginger add antioxidant compounds that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Spicy heat
items.content: Excessive Szechuan pepper can irritate the stomach in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Soy sauce allergy
items.content: People allergic to soy should use a soy‑free alternative.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce raises sodium levels, so those with hypertension should limit portion size.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot as a side dish with rice, noodles, or incorporate into stir‑fry bowls. Sprinkle with peanuts or sesame seeds for extra crunch and garnish with fresh cilantro.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked beans in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat in a pan or microwave with a splash of water to retain moisture.

peanut-butter-and-jelly-sandwich-with-re.title: Peanut Butter and Jelly Sandwich on Wheat Bread

content.title: About
content.content: The sandwich consists of two slices of wheat bread, a thin layer of reduced‑fat peanut butter, and sweet fruit jelly. It is a classic American snack that combines protein, carbohydrates, and a modest amount of fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Reduced‑fat peanut butter typically contains about 30 % fat instead of the 50 % found in regular versions.
Wheat bread retains more fiber and micronutrients than white bread.
The peanut butter & jelly sandwich appeared in the United States in the early 20th century and gained popularity after World War II.
The sweet‑salty flavor balance is considered ideal by many nutritionists.
Some U.S. schools ban peanut butter sandwiches because of allergy concerns.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Peanut butter provides about 8 g of protein per serving, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains heart‑healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: Even with reduced fat, the remaining monounsaturated fats can help maintain cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Wheat bread adds fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both the bread and the jelly supply thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Lower glycemic impact with no‑added‑sugar jelly
items.content: Choosing a jelly without added sugar results in a more moderate blood‑sugar response compared with conventional jams.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanut butter can trigger severe allergic reactions in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Sugar content in jelly
items.content: Traditional jelly often contains a lot of added sugar, increasing calories and affecting glucose levels.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Even with reduced fat, the sandwich remains relatively calorie‑dense; portion size should fit within daily energy goals.

items.title: Sodium in reduced‑fat peanut butter
items.content: Some low‑fat versions add salt; those monitoring sodium intake should choose a no‑salt option.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spread a thin layer of peanut butter on one slice of bread, evenly spread jelly on the other, and press together. The sandwich is easy to eat by hand, or cut into halves or quarters for children.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the assembled sandwich in an airtight container at room temperature for no more than 4 hours. Store opened peanut butter and jelly in the refrigerator, and keep bread in a dry place.

content.title: About
content.content: Seafood Sauce (1250) is a ready‑to‑use aromatic sauce made from tomatoes, fish stock, seaweed extract and spices. It is designed for quick preparation of dishes with fish, shrimp, mussels and other seafood, giving them a rich marine flavor and a mild heat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The formula often includes seaweed extract, which contributes a distinctive umami taste.
The recipe is inspired by Mediterranean cuisine, where tomato‑based fish sauces have been used for over 500 years.
The sauce can be used not only in hot dishes but also as a marinade for cold seafood appetizers.
Natural flavorings help retain many of the beneficial trace minerals found in marine fish.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Contains fish oil rich in omega‑3 fatty acids, which support heart and vascular health.

items.title: Source of iodine
items.content: Seaweed provides iodine, essential for normal thyroid function.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Compared with many ready sauces, this product has minimal added sugar.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Provides vitamin B12 and other B‑vitamins important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Tomatoes and spices supply lycopene and other antioxidants that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: The product may contain traces of fish, shellfish or shrimp, posing a risk for allergic individuals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The sauce has a moderate to high sodium level; people monitoring salt intake should use it sparingly.

items.title: Monosodium glutamate
items.content: Some versions contain added MSG; those sensitive to it should check the label.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add the sauce to a pan with sautéed seafood, simmer with vegetables, or use as a base for soups and risotto. It can also be mixed with sour cream or yogurt to create a dip for seafood appetizers.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the sauce in a sealed container in the refrigerator at 2 °C–6 °C. Once opened, keep it for up to 7 days. Discard if the smell, color or texture changes or if mold appears.

content.title: About
content.content: Welsh rarebit is a classic British dish consisting of toasted bread topped with a rich sauce made from melted cheese, mustard, beer and spices. It is usually served as a hot open‑face sandwich, sometimes garnished with herbs or tomato slices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “rarebit” is a humorous alteration of “rabbit”, although the dish contains no meat.
It originated in the 19th century and quickly became a staple in English pubs.
Traditional sauce uses cheddar cheese, but other cheeses such as gouda or Swiss can be used.
Worcestershire sauce and cayenne pepper are common additions for extra flavor.
Welsh rarebit is sometimes called “cheese on toast”, but the original sauce is thicker and more aromatic.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Cheese, the main ingredient, provides a high amount of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Cheese supplies complete protein that supports tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Cheese contains vitamin B12, which is important for nervous system function.

items.title: Benefits of mustard
items.content: Mustard adds selenium and antioxidants that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Moderate fat content
items.content: While cheese contains saturated fat, moderate portions can fit into a balanced diet.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The dairy components may cause discomfort for people who are lactose intolerant.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Cheese and Worcestershire sauce can be salty, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to milk proteins should avoid the dish.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish is relatively high in calories due to cheese and butter, so portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve Welsh rarebit hot, straight from the oven. Garnish with fresh herbs, tomato slices, or a sprinkle of paprika. It pairs well with a light salad or vegetable side.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Prepared sauce can be kept in the refrigerator for up to 2 days in an airtight container. Use fresh bread; if it has dried out, lightly toast it before adding the sauce.
